marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q001.takeaway: Each pharyngeal arch has a mesenchymal core formed by mesoderm and invading neural crest cells.
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q001.displayText:
Each pharyngeal arch is covered externally by ectoderm and lined internally by endoderm. Between them is a mesenchymal core derived from paraxial and lateral plate mesoderm and populated by neural crest cells.

Neural crest cells contribute much of the skeletal and connective tissue of the head and neck, while mesoderm contributes muscular and vascular components of the arch.

rationales.a: Ectoderm covers the outer surface of the arch; it is not one of the two principal cellular components of the mesenchymal core.
rationales.b: Endoderm lines the inner surface of the pharyngeal apparatus rather than forming the mesenchymal core.
rationales.d: Ectoderm and endoderm form the outer and inner epithelial coverings, respectively; the core is mesoderm plus neural crest cells.

marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q002.takeaway: The 5th pharyngeal arch is rudimentary and disappears soon after formation.
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q002.displayText:
Pharyngeal arches appear during the 4th–5th weeks and are numbered I–VI in craniocaudal order. The 5th arch is transient and disappears, leaving the functional arches I, II, III, IV and VI.

The 1st arch is the mandibular arch and the 2nd is the hyoid arch.

rationales.a: The 3rd arch persists and forms characteristic skeletal, muscular, arterial and neural derivatives.
rationales.b: The 4th arch persists and contributes to pharyngeal/laryngeal structures; it does not normally disappear soon after formation.
rationales.d: The 6th arch persists and contributes importantly to laryngeal structures and pulmonary-artery derivatives.

marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q003.takeaway: A pharyngeal membrane forms where an ectodermal cleft directly meets an endodermal pouch.
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q003.displayText:
Between adjacent arches, ectoderm dips inward as a pharyngeal cleft while endoderm evaginates outward as a pharyngeal pouch. Their point of contact forms a pharyngeal membrane.

Of the four pharyngeal membranes, only the 1st persists and contributes to the tympanic membrane; the others are obliterated as the 2nd arch overgrows the caudal arches.

rationales.a: A pharyngeal cleft is the ectodermal indentation between adjacent arches, not the ectoderm–endoderm contact itself.
rationales.b: A pharyngeal pouch is an endodermal outpocketing from the pharynx; the membrane forms where a pouch meets a cleft.
rationales.d: The cervical sinus is a temporary ectoderm-lined cavity created when the 2nd arch overgrows the lower clefts; it is not the cleft–pouch contact.

marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q004.takeaway: Mandibular hypoplasia with middle-ear or tympanic abnormalities points to a 1st pharyngeal apparatus developmental defect.
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q004.displayText:
The 1st pharyngeal (mandibular) arch gives rise to Meckel-cartilage derivatives and first-arch mesenchymal structures, including the mandible and major parts of the maxillary region. Its associated muscles include the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

The 1st pharyngeal pouch forms the auditory tube and middle-ear cavity, and the 1st membrane contributes to the tympanic membrane. A combined mandibular and middle-ear or tympanic defect therefore localizes to the first pharyngeal apparatus.

rationales.b: The 2nd arch is associated with Reichert cartilage, muscles of facial expression and the facial nerve; it does not explain the characteristic first-arch mandibular pattern.
rationales.c: The 3rd arch forms the greater horn/lower body of the hyoid and stylopharyngeus with glossopharyngeal innervation, not the mandibular apparatus.
rationales.d: The 6th arch chiefly contributes intrinsic laryngeal muscles and laryngeal cartilages with recurrent laryngeal innervation, not mandibular and middle-ear development.

marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q005.takeaway: Treacher Collins syndrome is a first-arch neural-crest disorder causing mandibulofacial hypoplasia and ear abnormalities.
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q005.displayText:
Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) reflects abnormal development of the 1st pharyngeal arch due to impaired neural crest contribution. Typical findings include hypoplasia of the mandible and zygomatic bones, malformed external ears or auditory-canal abnormalities, and downward-slanting palpebral fissures.

Pierre Robin sequence is related by mandibular hypoplasia but is classically a sequence of micrognathia → glossoptosis → cleft palate.

rationales.b: The 2nd arch is not the primary embryologic defect in Treacher Collins syndrome; its classic problem is abnormal first-arch cranial neural crest development.
rationales.c: The 3rd arch principally contributes to the hyoid/stylopharyngeus complex and is not the arch implicated in Treacher Collins syndrome.
rationales.d: The 6th arch contributes mainly to laryngeal development and is not the source of the mandibulofacial dysostosis pattern.

marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q006.takeaway: The stapes is a 2nd-arch (Reichert cartilage) derivative; it is not derived from Meckel cartilage.
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q006.displayText:
Meckel cartilage is the cartilage of the 1st pharyngeal arch. Its derivatives include the malleus, incus, anterior ligament of the malleus, spine of sphenoid and sphenomandibular ligament.

The stapes is derived from the 2nd pharyngeal arch cartilage (Reichert cartilage), making it the exception.

rationales.a: The malleus is a classic derivative of Meckel cartilage from the 1st pharyngeal arch.
rationales.b: The incus is also derived from Meckel cartilage of the 1st arch.
rationales.d: The sphenomandibular ligament develops from the perichondrium/remnant of Meckel cartilage and is therefore a 1st-arch derivative.

marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q007.takeaway: The stylohyoid ligament is derived from Reichert cartilage of the 2nd pharyngeal arch.
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q007.displayText:
Reichert cartilage is the cartilage of the 2nd pharyngeal arch. Its dorsal derivatives include the stapes, styloid process and stylohyoid ligament; its ventral derivatives form the lesser cornu and upper part of the body of the hyoid.

Elongation of the styloid process or calcification of the stylohyoid ligament can produce Eagle syndrome, with throat or facial pain and swallowing-related symptoms.

rationales.a: The 1st arch contains Meckel cartilage, which gives rise to structures such as malleus, incus and the sphenomandibular ligament—not the stylohyoid ligament.
rationales.c: The 3rd arch cartilage forms the greater cornu and lower body of the hyoid rather than the stylohyoid ligament.
rationales.d: The 4th arch contributes to laryngeal/pharyngeal structures and does not form the stylohyoid ligament.

marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q008.takeaway: The 3rd pharyngeal arch forms the greater cornu and lower part of the body of the hyoid.
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q008.displayText:
The cartilage of the 3rd pharyngeal arch forms the greater cornu of the hyoid and the lower part of the hyoid body.

By contrast, the lesser cornu and upper part of the hyoid body are derivatives of the 2nd arch.
emphasis: lower part of the hyoid body

rationales.a: The 2nd arch forms the lesser cornu and upper part of the hyoid body, not the greater cornu.
rationales.c: The 4th arch contributes chiefly to pharyngeal/laryngeal derivatives rather than the greater horn of the hyoid.
rationales.d: The hyoid has mixed arch origin: its upper body is 2nd-arch derived, whereas the lower body and greater cornu are 3rd-arch derived.

marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q009.takeaway: Tensor tympani is a 1st-arch muscle and is supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
marrow__ANAT_CH05_Q009.displayText:
The nerve of the 1st pharyngeal arch is the trigeminal nerve, with motor supply carried chiefly through its mandibular division (V3). First-arch muscles therefore include the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

Among the alternatives, stylopharyngeus is a 3rd-arch muscle (CN IX), posterior belly of digastric is a 2nd-arch muscle (CN VII), and levator veli palatini is a 4th-arch derivative supplied through the pharyngeal plexus.

rationales.a: Stylopharyngeus is the characteristic muscle of the 3rd arch and is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not V3.
rationales.c: The posterior belly of digastric is a 2nd-arch muscle supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
rationales.d: Levator veli palatini is associated with the 4th arch and receives motor supply through the pharyngeal plexus, chiefly via the vagus nerve, rather than V3.
